abstract: |
  For the last two decades, the gradient projection algorithm (GPA) has been the most used tool to rotate factor solutions. However, GPA is currently limited to performing either full orthogonal or oblique rotations. This is a shortcoming because in some cases it is known in advance that some factor correlations must be zero but keeping structural zeros in the factor correlation matrix after rotation is currently unavailable in Exploratory Factor Analysis. Thereby, we developed a new kind of rotation, the orthoblique rotation, in which both oblique and orthogonal relations between factors coexists. Building on the orthogonal and oblique algorithms of Jennrich, we provide a deeper account of how GPA works and use this account to generalize factor rotation to the orthoblique case. We then demonstrate that this rotation helps to estimate exploratory bi-factor models with multiple general factors in which the general factors may be correlated but must remain orthogonal to the group factors, which can be considered a generalization of the biquartimin and bigeomin criteria. We also illustrate its application to exploratory multitrait-multimethod models, where trait and method factors may correlate within their respective sets but trait–method correlations are constrained to zero. Taken together, this work can be seen as a continuation of the efforts of Jennrich to broaden the reach and flexibility of Exploratory Factor Analysis. Finally, we made available the new orthoblique rotation in the R package \texttt{latent}, whose \texttt{lrotate()} function serves the same purpose as the \texttt{GPArotation} package of Bernaards and Jennrich (2005).

# Introduction

Exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM) is an increasingly popular framework for estimating large and complex factor structures. It was developed to overcome the overly restrictive measurement models and the unacceptable model fit indices often encountered in real applications of confirmatory factor analysis (CFA; Marsh et al., 2020). The particular feature of ESEM is that it permits the estimation of all the loading parameters of the measurement models by means of a rotation step, reducing the risk of model misspecification. This way, ESEM avoids incorrectly fixing cross-loadings to zero in the measurement model, which is an important caveat of CFA.

However, the flexibility of ESEM comes at the expense of specifying a suitable simplicity or parsimony criterion to be optimized, so that a factor solution is rotated to a loading matrix that best approximates the desired simple structure. In this regard, the gradient projection algorithm (GPA; Jennrich, 2001; Jennrich, 2002) has been the predominant computational tool for rotating loading patterns during the last twenty years. The success of GPA is instantiated by its availability in widely used and reputed statistical programs such as Mplus [@mplus], \texttt{lavaan} [@lavaan], and \texttt{psych} [@psych]. In contrast with previously used rotation procedures like the criterion-specific pairwise algorithms discussed by @jennrich_2001, GPA is simple and elegant. In fact, a general-purpose optimization based on GPA can be written in about 50 lines of code in the R language ^[See the \texttt{GPForth} and \texttt{GPFoblq} functions from the \texttt{GPArotation} R package [@bernaards_2005] for orthogonal and oblique rotation, respectively.]. Moreover, GPA is based on an optimization framework where traditional step-size selection techniques (e.g., backtracking line-search or trust-region) and search directions based on first- and second-order derivatives can be used [@liu_2020].

The generality of GPA for factor rotation was the main contribution of @jennrich_2001 and @jennrich_2002. Rather than developing a different algorithm for every simplicity criterion, these papers showed that a common computational procedure could optimize many criteria under the same rotation constraints. Bernaards and Jennrich (2005) developed this idea into general-purpose software and separated the evaluation of the criterion and its gradient from the operations that enforce the rotation constraints. They also provided derivations, proofs, and software implementation details. Thus, their work provides both the computational starting point and the motivation for the present generalization. However, our purpose is to give a deeper and more explicit geometric account of all the mathematical objects involving factor rotation and the connections between them. Explaining why these operations are needed, how they are derived from the constraints of the rotation matrix, and how they work together provides a constructive route from the orthogonal and oblique cases to other rotation geometries.

This generalization is very important because in ESEM, the applications of GPA are currently limited to either orthogonal and oblique rotation. In other words, all the factors in ESEM are currenlty either constrained to be orthogonal or allowed to correlate. This circumstance is problematic in cases where the researchers know in advance that two sets of factors may be correlated within each set but orthogonal between sets. For example, consider multitrait-multimethod models, in which trait and method factors may correlate within their respective sets but trait–method correlations are constrained to zero. In this scenario, there should be structural zeros in the factor correlation matrix to effectively separate the variance explained by traits and methods. In other cases, it may be desirable to constrain one factor, or a group of factors, to be orthogonal to the remaining factors in order to obtain a more parsimonious pattern structure. For instance, consider applications of exploratory bi-factor modeling with one or multiple general factors in which all the general factors must be orthogonal to the group factors, but may be correlated among themselves [@jennrich_2012; @jimenez_2023a]. If the general factors were allowed to correlate with the group factors in an oblique rotation analysis, then the variance explained by each kind of factor could not be correctly disentangled, with the consequence that cross-loadings across the general factors would be biased.

Thereby, a generalization of the oblique and orthogonal rotations that allows for a mix of oblique and orthogonal factors within the same ESEM model could aid the correct estimation of such factor structures.

The objectives of this work are fourfold. First, we give a coherent and self-contained explanation of GPA for orthogonal and oblique rotation, connecting the matrix formulas of @jennrich_2001, @jennrich_2002, and Bernaards and Jennrich (2005) with their underlying geometry. Second, using these explanations, we derive the orthoblique manifold and show how the conventional rotations are obtained as special cases. Third, we make these new rotation capabilities available in the \texttt{latent} package and explain how \texttt{lrotate()} extends the rotation framework represented by \texttt{GPArotation}. Lastly, we illustrate the usefulness of this generalization in exploratory multitrait-multimethod and bifactor models with the idea of retaining the flexibility of ESEM to uncover cross-loadings and wrong theoretical expectations while retaining certain factor-correlation restrictions.

# Factor rotation

Because rotation is applied only to measurement parameters, without loss of generality we will consider the simplest case of ESEM: Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA). EFA is usually performed in two steps. First, an identified model $\hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_0\mathbf{\Lambda}_0^\top + \mathbf{\Theta}$ is estimated by maximum likelihood or least squares by constraining $\mathbf{\Lambda}_0$ to have either orthogonal columns or a lower-triangular structure. Second, $\mathbf{\Lambda}_0$ is rotated to find an equally fitting model $\hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{\Psi}\mathbf{\Lambda}^\top + \mathbf{\Theta}$, where $\mathbf{\Lambda} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_0\mathbf{X}^{-\top}$ and $\mathbf{\Psi} = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is the latent factor correlation matrix. This last step involves finding the optimal rotation matrix $\mathbf{X}$ that minimizes a complexity criterion seeking to obtain a sparse and interpretable $\mathbf{\Lambda}$. However, $\mathbf{X}$ must be subject to certain constraints that distinguish orthogonal from oblique rotations. In orthogonal rotation, the constraint is $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}$, whereas in oblique rotation it is $\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{1}$. Therefore, both orthogonal and oblique rotation matrices belong to smooth nonlinear sets of $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ matrices characterized by these specific constraints. Informally, these specific sets are termed manifolds and denoted by $\mathcal{M}$.

The problem of factor rotation is that the optimal orthogonal or oblique rotation matrix $\mathbf{X}$ cannot generally be found by using ordinary optimization algorithms that do not enforce these constraints. For this purpose, the Gradient Projection Algorithm (GPA) has proved to be an elegant and robust solution. GPA builds on differential geometry to perform optimization on nonlinear manifolds. Let $\tilde{f}$ be a complexity function with domain in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ that we aim to minimize with respect to a rotation matrix $\mathbf{X}$. This function can be any complexity criterion, such as varimax, oblimin, or geomin. Suppose that we want to constrain the solution to lie on a nonlinear manifold $\mathcal{M}$ characterized by a defining smooth function $h:\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}$ that satisfies

$$
\mathcal{M} = h^{-1}(\mathbf{0}) = \left\{ \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: h(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{0} \right\},
$$

so that any matrix $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}$ implies $h(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{0}$. Here, $d$ is the number of independent constraints defining the manifold. This means that, in the orthogonal case, $h$ collects the $n(n+1)/2$ distinct constraints of the symmetric matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{I}$, whereas in the oblique case it collects the $n$ diagonal constraints. In this manner, the orthogonal and oblique manifolds can be stated as the sets of full-rank $\mathbf{X}$ matrices satisfying the following conditions, respectively:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{O}(n) &= \left\{ \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: h(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{0} \right\}, \\
\mathcal{OB}(n) &= \left\{ \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: h(\mathbf{X}) = \mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})-\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0} \right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

<!-- Because these constraints are smooth and their differentials have full rank at every point of the manifolds, the regular level-set theorem guarantees that these sets are smooth embedded manifolds.^[That is, $\mathrm{rank}(\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}))=d$ for all $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}$ [@boumal_2023, Sections 3.2 and 7.7].] -->

To better understand these manifold definitions, an illustration of the orthogonal and oblique manifolds for $n=3$ is presented in Figure 1. In both manifolds, each column $\mathbf{x}_j$ of the rotation matrix is a unit vector and can therefore be represented on the unit sphere. The oblique manifold is the product of $n$ unit spheres, whereas the orthogonal manifold is the subset of this product in which the vectors are also constrained to point in mutually perpendicular directions.

Visually, the GPA consists of moving these vectors across the surface of the unit sphere until the complexity criterion $\tilde{f}$ is minimized, subject to the additional perpendicularity constraints in orthogonal rotation. To move the vectors in this way while minimizing $\tilde{f}$, small steps must be taken through an iterative algorithm. However, this is not trivial. At iteration $k$, traditional unconstrained optimization algorithms usually compute a new candidate as
$$
\mathbf{X}_{k+1} = \mathbf{X}_k + t_k\mathbf{V}_k,
$$ {#eq-updating}

where $\mathbf{V}_k$ is a direction along which the complexity function decreases and $t_k$ is a step size. In gradient descent, for example, $\mathbf{V}_k = -\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}_k)$, where $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}_k)$ is the Euclidean gradient in the unrestricted space $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$.^[The Euclidean gradient is characterized by $\mathrm{D}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}_k)[\mathbf{V}] = \langle \mathbf{V},\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}_k)\rangle$ for any $\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, with $\langle ., . \rangle$ denoting the Frobenius inner product.] The problem is that this updating scheme does not guarantee that the new candidate $\mathbf{X}_{k+1}$ remains on the manifold, not even when $\mathbf{X}_k$ already belongs to it. Furthermore, the descent direction $\mathbf{V}_k$ is also unrestricted in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and is not necessarily a valid descent direction on a nonlinear manifold. In other words, a straight-line displacement in the Euclidean space, as shown in the updating @eq-updating, is not generally a feasible displacement on a nonlinear manifold.

Hence, the GPA solves two problems: (1) proposing an appropriate descent direction $\mathbf{V}_k$ on $\mathcal{M}$ and (2) securing that, after moving along this direction, the new candidate $\mathbf{X}_{k+1}$ remains on $\mathcal{M}$.

# Solution to problem 1: the Riemannian gradient

To address the first problem, we replace the unrestricted Euclidean gradient with its counterpart on the manifold. For the restricted criterion $f=\tilde{f}|_{\mathcal{M}}$, the Riemannian gradient lies in the tangent space and represents how the criterion changes along first-order feasible directions. Its negative is a descent direction whenever the gradient is nonzero. More precisely, it is characterized as follows [@boumal_2023, Definition 3.58].

\begin{definition}
The Riemannian gradient of $f$ at $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}$, denoted by $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})$, is the unique element of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$ that satisfies $\mathrm{D}f(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}] = \left\langle \mathbf{V}, \text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}) \right\rangle_{\mathbf{X}}$ for every $\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$.
\end{definition}

<!-- \left[ -->
<!-- -\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}) -->
<!-- \right] -->
<!-- &= -->

<!-- The inequality is strict whenever $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})\neq\mathbf{0}$. Therefore, the first task of the GPA is to replace the negative Euclidean gradient with the negative Riemannian gradient, which is a valid tangent descent direction. -->

Informally, if we zoom in enough around a point $\mathbf{X} \in \mathcal{M}$, eventually everything looks linear.^[As an analogy, the Earth is round but locally everything looks flat.] Thus, an idea to move over $\mathcal{M}$ consists of finding tangent directions to $\mathbf{X} \in \mathcal{M}$ that look linear from an infinitesimal point of view. 

Consider doing a first-order Taylor expansion of $h$ around the current candidate $\mathbf{X}_k$,
$$
h(\mathbf{X}_k+t\mathbf{V}_k) \approx h(\mathbf{X}_k) + t\,\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}_k)[\mathbf{V}_k].
$$ {#eq-taylor}
Because we can always propose a candidate $\mathbf{X}_k$ that already belongs to $\mathcal{M}$ ^[We can always propose an initial starting point $\mathbf{X}_1 \in \mathcal{M}$.], it follows that $h(\mathbf{X}_k) = \mathbf{0}$. Then, we may choose a $\mathbf{V}_k$ such that $\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}_k)[\mathbf{V}_k] = \mathbf{0}$, so that @eq-taylor becomes $\mathbf{0}$ and we preserve the manifold constraints to first order. Therefore, appropriate directions to move along the manifolds constitute the kernel of $\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}_k)$:
$$
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M} \equiv \ker\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X}) = \left\{ \mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: \mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}] = \mathbf{0} \right\},
$$
where the subscript $k$ is dropped hereafter for clarity and generality. The set $\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}$ is known as the tangent space of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathcal{M}$. In other words, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$ is the set of all infinitesimally feasible directions at $\mathbf{X}$ that are linear. This linearity property is important because it allows traditional optimization algorithms that work in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ to be used in the GPA framework.

Connecting this new notion of linear space to our previous examples, the tangent spaces of the orthogonal and oblique manifolds at any $\mathbf{X} \in \mathcal{M}$ can be stated as the collection of directions for which the differentials of their respective defining functions are $\mathbf{0}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{O}(n) &= \left\{ \mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0} \right\}, \\
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{OB}(n) &= \left\{ \mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: \mathrm{ddiag}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{0} \right\},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-tangent_space}
where $\mathrm{ddiag}$ is an operator that sets the off-diagonal entries of a matrix to zero.

Notice that tangent spaces can be viewed as a collection of the $n^2-d$ free components in the manifolds, so that $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{O}(n)) = n(n-1)/2$ is the number of free elements in an orthogonal matrix and $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{OB}(n)) = n(n-1)$ is the number of free elements in an oblique matrix. Thereby, we can exploit the above differentials to parameterize the tangent spaces in such a way that the parameterizations preserve the tangent space dimension.

In the orthogonal case, for instance, if we set $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X\Omega}$, then by substitution in @eq-tangent_space, we have
$$
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{O}(n) = \left\{ \mathbf{X\Omega}: \mathbf{\Omega} + \mathbf{\Omega}^\top = \mathbf{0} \right\}.
$$
This is a valid full-rank parameterization of the tangent space of the orthogonal manifold because $\mathbf{\Omega}$ is a skew-symmetric matrix and hence it has $n(n-1)/2$ free elements.

In the oblique case, for a nonsingular rotation matrix $\mathbf{X}$, a useful full-rank parameterization of the tangent space is $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X}^{-\top} \mathbf{\Omega}$, which by substitution in @eq-tangent_space, yields
$$
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{OB}(n)
=
\left\{
\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}:
\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{\Omega})
=
\mathbf{0}
\right\}.
$$
Indeed, $\mathbf{\Omega}$ is an arbitrary off-diagonal matrix with $n(n-1)$ free elements and thus it is a valid full-rank basis of the tangent space of the oblique manifold.

Now, notice that any member of $\mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ can be decomposed in orthogonal complements. At any point $\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}$, the Euclidean space can be decomposed into the orthogonal direct sum of the tangent and normal spaces,
$$
\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
=
\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}
\oplus
\mathcal{N}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}.
$$ {#eq-orth_compl}

If this $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ element is the Euclidean gradient of $\tilde{f}$ at $\mathbf{X}$, this means that it can be decomposed into an element belonging to the tangent space, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$, and another belonging to the normal space, $\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$. Therefore, there must exist orthogonal complements satisfying

$$
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}) = \text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\parallel + \text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp,
$$ {#eq-orth_compl_grad}

where $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\parallel$ and $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp$ are the projections of $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})$ onto the tangent and normal spaces of the manifold $\mathcal{M}$, respectively [@absil_2009, p. 47]. Figure 2 depicts the relationship between these quantities.

\centering

As it can be seen in Figure 2, a tangent space is indeed a linearization of the manifold at a given $\mathbf{X}$ and for any vector in the tangent space there would be another vector from the normal space that is orthogonal to it and satisfies @eq-orth_compl. However, to make sense of this notion of orthogonality at any $\mathbf{V} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$, we must endow the tangent space with a metric like the Frobenius inner product (i.e., $\langle \mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}} = \text{trace}(\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{V})$), so that $\mathcal{M}$ acquires a Riemannian structure, turning it into a Riemannian manifold. In other words, the collection of inner products on the tangent spaces defines a Riemannian metric on $\mathcal{M}$, turning it into a Riemannian manifold. And this definition of inner product over the tangent space of $\mathcal{M}$ allows us to develop a definition of orthogonal complements.

Recall that $f=\tilde{f}|_{\mathcal{M}}$ is the restriction of the complexity criterion to the manifold. Using @eq-orth_compl_grad and the Frobenius inner product as Riemannian metric, we arrive at the following identities for any $\mathbf{V} \in \mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}$: 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\langle
\mathbf{V},
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\parallel
\right\rangle_{\mathbf{X}}
&=
\mathrm{trace}\left[
\mathbf{V}^\top
\left(
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp
\right)
\right]
\\
&=
\mathrm{trace}\left(
\mathbf{V}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right)
-
\mathrm{trace}\left(
\mathbf{V}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp
\right)
\\
&=
\mathrm{trace}\left(
\mathbf{V}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right),
\quad
\text{because }
\mathbf{V}
\text{ is orthogonal to }
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp,
\\
&=
\mathrm{D}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}],
\quad
\text{by the definition of the Euclidean gradient},
\\
&=
\mathrm{D}f(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}],
\quad
\text{because }
f=\tilde{f}|_{\mathcal{M}}
\text{ and }
\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M} \\
&= \left\langle
\mathbf{V},
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
\right\rangle_{\mathbf{X}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality follows directly from the definition of the Riemannian gradient. And from the preceding identities, this element turns out to be $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\parallel$, the projection of the Euclidean gradient onto the tangent space of $\mathcal{M}$.

There can be many ways to find the Riemannian gradient, but a good strategy consists of obtaining an expression for $\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})_\perp \in \mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$ and substituting this into @eq-orth_compl_grad.

In the case of the orthogonal and oblique manifolds, the parameterizations of the tangent spaces were $\mathbf{X\Omega}$ and $\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}$, respectively, so the normal spaces must be
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{O}(n)
&=
\left\{
\mathbf{N}:
\mathbf{N}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A},
\quad
\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{A}^\top
\right\},
\\
\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{OB}(n)
&=
\left\{
\mathbf{N}:
\mathbf{N}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A},
\quad
\mathbf{A}
\text{ is diagonal}
\right\},
\end{aligned}
$$ 
respectively. Clearly, the tangent and normal parameterizations are orthogonal in each scenario.^[$\langle \mathbf{X\Omega}, \mathbf{XA} \rangle = 0$ for a skew-symmetric $\mathbf{\Omega}$ and symmetric $\mathbf{A}$ (orthogonal manifold) and $\langle \mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}, \mathbf{XA} \rangle = 0$ for an off-diagonal $\mathbf{\Omega}$ and diagonal $\mathbf{A}$ (oblique manifold).] Therefore, in both cases the Riemannian gradient can be written as
$$
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
=
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A},
$$ {#eq-riemannian_param}
where $\mathbf{A}$ must be chosen so that $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})$ belongs to the corresponding tangent space.

For orthogonal rotation, the Riemannian gradient must satisfy the tangent space equation
$$
\mathbf{X}^\top\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
+
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})^\top\mathbf{X}
=
\mathbf{0}.
$$

Substituting $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})$ by the orthogonal complements parameterization in @eq-riemannian_param gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X}^\top
\left(
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
\right)
+
\left(
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
\right)^\top
\mathbf{X}
&= \mathbf{0}
\\
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
+
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})^\top
\mathbf{X}
-
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
-
\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}
&= \mathbf{0}, \quad \text{and}
\\
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
+
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})^\top
\mathbf{X}
-
2\mathbf{A}
&= \mathbf{0}, \quad \text{because } \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{I} \text{ and } \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{A}^\top.
\end{aligned}
$$
It then follows that
$$
\mathbf{A}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
+
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})^\top
\mathbf{X}
\right].
$$

Finally, defining $\mathrm{sym}(\mathbf{B})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{B}^\top\right)$, we have $\mathbf{A}=\mathrm{sym}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})\right)$ and the Riemannian gradient for orthogonal rotation becomes
$$
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}) = \text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}) -
\mathbf{X}\, \mathrm{sym}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top \text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X}) \right).
$$

On the other hand, for oblique rotation, the Riemannian gradient must satisfy the tangent space equation
$$
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
\right]
=
\mathbf{0}.
$$

Substituting again $\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})$ for the orthogonal complements parameterization in @eq-riemannian_param gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\left(
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
\right)
\right]
&= \mathbf{0}
\\
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right]
-
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left(
\mathbf{X}^\top
\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}
\right)
&= \mathbf{0}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Because $\mathbf{A}$ is diagonal and $\mathrm{ddiag}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\right)=\mathbf{I}$, we get $\mathbf{A} = \mathrm{ddiag}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}\right)$.

Therefore,
$$
\mathbf{A}
=
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right],
$$

and the Riemannian gradient for oblique rotation becomes
$$
\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X})
=
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
-
\mathbf{X}
\mathrm{ddiag}
\left[
\mathbf{X}^\top
\text{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})
\right].
$$

These are indeed the same projected gradients formulas denoted by \texttt{Gp} in the orthogonal and oblique implementations of @bernaards_2005 [pp. 692--695] and in the \texttt{GPArotation} package.

# Solution to problem 2: the Retraction

With this generalization of gradients to nonlinear manifolds, we are prepared to compute valid descent directions in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{M}$. However, we are not ready yet because the update
$$
\mathbf{X}_{k+1} = \mathbf{X}_k-t_k\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}_k)
$$

does not generally belong to $\mathcal{M}$, however small $t_k$ is. The tangent direction only provides a first-order linear approximation to the manifold at $\mathbf{X}_k$, as we showed before in @eq-taylor. This means that the condition $\mathrm{D}h(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}]=\mathbf{0}$ does not generally imply that the tangent step $\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V}$ lies exactly on $\mathcal{M}$ for a nonzero $t$. It only ensures that the constraints are preserved to first order. To see this, let's take the crossproduct of the tangent step to check how it departs from the orthogonal manifold constraints:
$$
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V})^\top (\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V}) &= \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + t(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{X}) + t^2\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V} \\
&= \mathbf{I} + t^2\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here, the factor $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{X}$ vanishes because $\mathbf{V}$ was chosen precisely to satisfy the tangent equation for the orthogonal manifold (@eq-tangent_space). The orthogonality constraint is therefore violated by the residual $t^2\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V}$. Following the same argument in the case of the oblique manifold, we would have found that the unit norm constraint is off by a factor of $t^2\text{ddiag}(\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V})$. 

Thereby, mapping the tangent step back to the manifold is the second problem addressed by the GPA. After taking a step $t$ along the negative Riemannian gradient, the resulting point must be projected back onto the manifold while preserving the initial direction of the tangent step. 

Suppose that we apply some projection $R_\mathbf{X}:\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}$ that restores the constraints exactly. Because the tangent step is already correct to first order, $R_\mathbf{X}$ only needs to act on the higher-order residuals. This is exactly what a retraction does: it fixes the constraints of the tangent step without modifying the descent direction, which in the GPA is the negative of the Riemannian gradient.

\begin{definition}
\label{retraction_definition}
A retraction is a smooth map
$R_\mathbf{X}:\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}$ that satisfies the following conditions: \\
(1) $R_\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{X}$, and \\
(2) $DR_\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{0})[\mathbf{V}]=\mathbf{V}$ for every
$\mathbf{V}\in\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}$, so that
$DR_\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{0})$ is the identity map on
$\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{X}\mathcal{M}$.
\end{definition}

A local retraction only needs to be defined for sufficiently small tangent steps, while satisfying the same two conditions. The first condition ensures that taking a zero step leaves the current point unchanged. The second condition recognizes that the tangent step $\mathbf{X} + t\mathbf{V}$ already satisfies the manifold constraints to first order because $\mathbf{V}$ was picked to satisfy the tangent space equations. Therefore it requires that $R_{\mathbf{X}}(t\mathbf{V})$ has the same initial direction $\mathbf{V}$ as the tangent step. In other words, a retraction restores the manifold constraints exactly without changing the first-order motion on the manifold so that the Riemannian gradient can still be used as the descent direction. 

<!-- Both requirements can equivalently be stated by considering the curve -->
<!-- $$ -->
<!-- \gamma(t)=R_\mathbf{X}(t\mathbf{V}), -->
<!-- $$ -->
<!-- which satisfies $\gamma(0)=\mathbf{X}$ and $\gamma^\prime(0)=\mathbf{V}$. -->

<!-- Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a smooth map from an ambient neighborhood of $\mathbf{X}$ into the manifold. Suppose that $\mathcal P(\mathbf{Y})=\mathbf{Y}$ for every nearby $\mathbf{Y} \in\mathcal M$. Then $R_{\mathbf X}(\mathbf V)=\mathcal P(\mathbf X+\mathbf V)$ defines a local retraction. Since $\mathcal P$ leaves manifold points unchanged, $\mathcal P(\gamma(t))=\gamma(t)$. Differentiating this identity at zero yields $\mathrm D\mathcal P(\mathbf X)[\mathbf V] = \mathbf V$. The chain rule then gives $\mathrm D R_{\mathbf X}(\mathbf0)[\mathbf V] = \mathrm D\mathcal P(\mathbf X)[\mathbf V] = \mathbf V$. Also, $R_{\mathbf X}(\mathbf0)=\mathcal P(\mathbf X)=\mathbf X$. That proves both conditions. -->

Combining the Riemannian gradient with a retraction, the valid updating equation that GPA uses becomes
$$
\mathbf{X}_{k+1} = R_{\mathbf{X}_k} \left(-t_k\text{grad}f(\mathbf{X}_k) \right).
$$ {#eq-gpa_update}

Hence, the Riemannian gradient determines a valid descent direction in the tangent space, whereas the retraction guarantees that the new candidate $\mathbf{X}_{k+1}$ belongs to $\mathcal{M}$ after correcting the higher-order imprecisions of the tangent step. Figure \ref{fig:retraction} illustrates how a tangent step is retracted onto the manifold.

For orthogonal rotation, a suitable retraction is obtained by applying the Gram-Schmidt algorithm to the columns of $\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{V}$. Equivalently, $R_\mathbf{X}^{\text{orth}}(\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{Q}$, where $\mathbf{Q}$ is the orthonormal matrix of the QR decomposition of $\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{V}$, with the triangular factor chosen to have positive diagonal entries. Alternatively, if $\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{W}^\top$ is a singular value decomposition, another valid retraction is $R_\mathbf{X}^{\text{orth}}(\mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{W}^\top$. This is actually the orthogonal projection used in the algorithms of @jennrich_2001 and @bernaards_2005. The QR and singular value decomposition retractions need not produce the same finite update, but both preserve tangent directions to first order and both are smooth operations satisfying the conditions in Definition \ref{retraction_definition}.

On the other hand, for oblique rotation, a suitable retraction involves just normalizing the columns of $\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{V}$: $R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathrm{oblq}}(\mathbf{V}) = (\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{V}) \left[\mathrm{ddiag}\!\left((\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{V})^\top (\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{V})\right)\right]^{-1/2}$, which is the manifold projection used by @jennrich_2002 [Appendix A.1].

# The orthoblique manifold

The orthoblique manifold encompasses a mixture of oblique and orthogonal relations between factors. Geometrically, in $n=3$ it consists of solving the same problem of orthogonal and oblique rotations by minimizing a complexity function while moving vectors on a sphere, with the difference that only one vector is required to be orthogonal to the others (Figure \ref{fig:orthoblique-manifold}).
