For clarity, we first consider the case of two blocks of oblique factors and another block of completely orthogonal factors. However, the following results can be generalized to any number of oblique blocks of factors.

Let $\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p,q\},r\big)$ denote the set of orthoblique matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ defined by

$$
\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p,q\},r\big)
=
\left\{
\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{Y}_1 & \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{0}\\
\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{Y}_2 & \mathbf{0}\\
\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I}
\end{bmatrix},
\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{Y}_1)=\mathbf{1},
\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{Y}_2)=\mathbf{1}
\right\},
$$
where $p$ is the number of oblique factors in the first block, $q$ is the number of oblique factors in the second block, $r$ is the number of completely orthogonal factors in the third block, and thus $n=p+q+r$. Let's partition $\mathbf{X}$ accordingly as $\mathbf{X}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{X}_1 & \mathbf{X}_2 & \mathbf{X}_3 \end{bmatrix}$, where $\mathbf{X}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$, $\mathbf{X}_2\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}$, and $\mathbf{X}_3\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}$. Then,
$$
\mathbf{Y}_1 = \mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_1, \qquad
\mathbf{Y}_2 = \mathbf{X}_2^\top\mathbf{X}_2, \qquad
\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{X}_3^\top\mathbf{X}_3.
$$

Thus, the factors in the oblique blocks $\mathbf{X}_1$ and $\mathbf{X}_2$ are oblique within but orthogonal in between. On the other hand, the factors in $\mathbf{X}_3$ are orthogonal both to each other and to the factors in the two oblique blocks.

The workflow to derive the Riemannian gradient of the orthoblique manifold is as follows: First, we find a smooth defining function $h$ to describe the manifold. Second, we develop a full-rank representation of the tangent and normal spaces in terms of $\mathbf{X}$. Third, using these parameterizations of the tangent and normal spaces, we find an expression for the projection of the Euclidean gradient of $\tilde{f}$ onto the tangent space. Fourth, we propose a retraction satisfying Definition \ref{retraction_definition}.

## Defining function

We can write the orthoblique manifold in terms of a defining function $h$ that collects the constraints in block-matrix form such that $\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p,q\},r\big) = \left\{ \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}: h(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{0} \right\}$, with

$$
h(\mathbf{X})
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathrm{ddiag}(\mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_1)-\mathbf{I}
&
\mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_2
&
\mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_3
\\
\mathbf{X}_2^\top\mathbf{X}_1
&
\mathrm{ddiag}(\mathbf{X}_2^\top\mathbf{X}_2)-\mathbf{I}
&
\mathbf{X}_2^\top\mathbf{X}_3
\\
\mathbf{X}_3^\top\mathbf{X}_1
&
\mathbf{X}_3^\top\mathbf{X}_2
&
\mathbf{X}_3^\top\mathbf{X}_3-\mathbf{I}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

As already explained, $h$ is understood to collect only the independent entries of this symmetric block matrix: the $p$ and $q$ diagonal constraints in the first two blocks, the entries in the three upper off-diagonal blocks, and the $r(r+1)/2$ distinct entries of the third diagonal block. Hence, the number of independent constraints is $d = p+q+pq+pr+qr+ r(r+1)/2$.

## Tangent space

The tangent space is obtained by differentiating the previous block-matrix representation of $\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p,q\}, r\big)$. First, let $\mathbf{V}$ be a tangent matrix with partitions $\mathbf{V} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{V}_1 & \mathbf{V}_2 & \mathbf{V}_3 \end{bmatrix}.$
Then, the tangent space can be represented as
$$
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}
\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p,q\},r\big)
= \left\{ 
\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathrm{ddiag}(\mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{V}_1)
&
\mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{V}_2+
\mathbf{V}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_2
&
\mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{V}_3+
\mathbf{V}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_3
\\
\mathbf{X}_2^\top\mathbf{V}_1+
\mathbf{V}_2^\top\mathbf{X}_1
&
\mathrm{ddiag}(\mathbf{X}_2^\top\mathbf{V}_2)
&
\mathbf{X}_2^\top\mathbf{V}_3+
\mathbf{V}_2^\top\mathbf{X}_3
\\
\mathbf{X}_3^\top\mathbf{V}_1+
\mathbf{V}_3^\top\mathbf{X}_1
&
\mathbf{X}_3^\top\mathbf{V}_2+
\mathbf{V}_3^\top\mathbf{X}_2
&
\mathbf{X}_3^\top\mathbf{V}_3+
\mathbf{V}_3^\top\mathbf{X}_3
\end{bmatrix}
=
\mathbf{0}
\right\}.
$$

At a nonsingular rotation matrix $\mathbf{X}$, we can parameterize this tangent space as $\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}$, where $\mathbf{\Omega}=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}$. Then, by substitution we have

$$
\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}
\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p,q\},r\big)
= \left\{ 
\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}: \begin{bmatrix}
\text{ddiag}(\mathbf{\Omega}_{11})
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{12} + \mathbf{\Omega}_{21}^\top
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{13} + \mathbf{\Omega}_{31}^\top
\\
\mathbf{\Omega}_{21} + \mathbf{\Omega}_{12}^\top
&
\text{ddiag}(\mathbf{\Omega}_{22})
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{23} + \mathbf{\Omega}_{32}^\top
\\
\mathbf{\Omega}_{31} + \mathbf{\Omega}_{13}^\top
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{32} + \mathbf{\Omega}_{23}^\top
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{33} + \mathbf{\Omega}_{33}^\top
\end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0}
\right\},
$$

where $\mathbf{\Omega}$ has the following block structure:
$$
\mathbf{\Omega} = \begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{\Omega}_{11}
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{12}
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{13}
\\
-\mathbf{\Omega}_{12}^\top
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{22}
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{23} 
\\
-\mathbf{\Omega}_{13}^\top
&
-\mathbf{\Omega}_{23}^\top
&
\mathbf{\Omega}_{33}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$
$\mathbf{\Omega}_{11}$ and $\mathbf{\Omega}_{22}$ can be arbitrary zero-diagonal matrices and $\mathbf{\Omega}_{33}$ must be skew-symmetric. The block matrices in the upper diagonal can be totally arbitrary, but the must be skew-symmetric with respect to the lower diagonal blocks. We can see that $\text{dim}(\mathbf{\Omega}) = p(p-1) + q(q-1) + pq + pr + qr + r(r-1)/2$. Indeed, this is the same than $n^2-d$ and hence $\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}$ is a valid full-rank basis of the tangent space.

## Normal space

Following the same principle as for the orthogonal and oblique manifolds, the normal space is the orthogonal complement of the tangent space. A valid parameterization can be constructed by stacking the orthogonal complements of the individual blocks of $\mathbf{\Omega}$. We already showed that any diagonal matrix is an orthogonal complement of any off-diagonal matrix and that any symmetric matrix is an orthogonal complement of any skew-symmetric matrix. Therefore,
$$
\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}
\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p,q\},r\big)
=
\left\{
\mathbf{N}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}:
\mathbf{A}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{D}_1
&
\mathbf{B}_{12}
&
\mathbf{B}_{13}
\\
\mathbf{B}_{12}^\top
&
\mathbf{D}_2
&
\mathbf{B}_{23}
\\
\mathbf{B}_{13}^\top
&
\mathbf{B}_{23}^\top
&
\mathbf{S}
\end{bmatrix}
\right\},
$$
where $\mathbf{D}_1$ and $\mathbf{D}_2$ are diagonal matrices, $\mathbf{S}$ is symmetric, and $\mathbf{B}_{12}$, $\mathbf{B}_{13}$, and $\mathbf{B}_{23}$ are unrestricted matrices with transposed counterparts below the diagonal.

Indeed, if $\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p,q\},r\big)$ and $\mathbf{N}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p,q\},r\big)$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle\mathbf{V},\mathbf{N}\rangle
&=
\mathrm{trace}
\left(
\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{N}
\right)
\\
&=
\mathrm{trace}
\left(
\mathbf{\Omega}^\top
\mathbf{X}^{-1}
\mathbf{X}
\mathbf{A}
\right)
\\
&=
\mathrm{trace}
\left(
\mathbf{\Omega}^\top\mathbf{A}
\right)
\\
&=
0,
\end{aligned}
$$
and the next step is to find the right $\mathbf{A}$ to construct an expression of the Riemannian gradient. 

## Riemannian gradient

For clarity, let $\mathbf{G} = \mathrm{grad}\tilde{f}(\mathbf{X})$ denote the Euclidean gradient. As in the orthogonal and oblique cases, the Riemannian gradient here is obtained by subtracting its normal component ([@eq-riemannian_param]), leaving $\mathrm{grad}f(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}$. The matrix $\mathbf{A}$ must be chosen so that $\mathrm{grad}f(\mathbf{X}) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}} \mathcal{POB}$. Hence, substituting $\mathbf{V}$ for this parameterization of the Riemannian gradient in the equation for the tangent space, all the components in the following symmetric matrix become $\mathbf{0}$:
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathrm{ddiag}\!\left(
\mathbf{X}_1^\top \mathbf{G}_1-\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{D}_1
\right)
&
\mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{G}_2
+\mathbf{G}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_2
-\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{B}_{12}
-\mathbf{B}_{12}\mathbf{Y}_2
&
\mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{G}_3
+\mathbf{G}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_3
-\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{B}_{13}
-\mathbf{B}_{13}
\\
&
\mathrm{ddiag}\!\left(
\mathbf{X}_2^\top \mathbf{G}_2-\mathbf{Y}_2\mathbf{D}_2
\right)
&
\mathbf{X}_2^\top\mathbf{G}_3
+\mathbf{G}_2^\top\mathbf{X}_3
-\mathbf{Y}_2\mathbf{B}_{23}
-\mathbf{B}_{23}
\\
&
&
\mathbf{X}_3^\top \mathbf{G}_3+ \mathbf{G}_3^\top \mathbf{X}_3 - 2\mathbf S
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Each block can now be solved separately.^[Notice that we omitted the lower triangle of the matrix because it is redundant with the transpose of the upper triangle.] Furthermore, the diagonal blocks of the above expression are the same equations as in the oblique and orthogonal demonstrations but represented in block format. Thereby, the unique $\mathbf{A}$ that satisfies @eq-riemannian_param becomes
$$
\mathbf{A} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{D}_1 = \mathrm{ddiag}\!\left( \mathbf{X}_1^\top \mathbf{G}_1 \right)
&
\mathbf{B}_{12}
&
\mathbf{B}_{13}
\\
\mathbf{B}_{12}^\top
&
\mathbf{D}_2 = \mathrm{ddiag}\!\left( \mathbf{X}_2^\top \mathbf{G}_2 \right)
&
\mathbf{B}_{23}
\\
\mathbf{B}_{13}^\top
&
\mathbf{B}_{23}^\top
&
\mathbf{S} = \text{sym}(\mathbf{X}_3^\top \mathbf{G}_3)
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For the submatrices at the intersection of the oblique and orthogonal blocks, the solutions are
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{B}_{13} &= (\mathbf{Y}_1 + \mathbf{I})^{-1}(\mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{G}_3 +\mathbf{G}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_3), \\
\mathbf{B}_{23} &= (\mathbf{Y}_2 + \mathbf{I})^{-1}(\mathbf{X}_2^\top\mathbf{G}_3 +\mathbf{G}_2^\top\mathbf{X}_3).
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the only remaining block is the intersection between the two oblique blocks, where
$$
\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{B}_{12} + \mathbf{B}_{12}\mathbf{Y}_2 = \mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{G}_2 + \mathbf{G}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_2.
$$

This is a Sylvester equation. Let $\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{X}_1^\top\mathbf{G}_2 + \mathbf{G}_1^\top\mathbf{X}_2$, $\mathbf{Y}_1 = \mathbf{U}_1\mathbf{V}_1\mathbf{U}_1^\top$, and $\mathbf{Y}_2 = \mathbf{U}_2\mathbf{V}_2\mathbf{U}_2^\top$, where the last two expressions are the eigendecompositions of the symmetric correlation matrices $\mathbf{Y}_1$ and $\mathbf{Y}_2$, respectively. Then, by substitution we have

$$
(\mathbf{U}_1\mathbf{V}_1\mathbf{U}_1^\top)\mathbf{B}_{12} + \mathbf{B}_{12}(\mathbf{U}_2\mathbf{V}_2\mathbf{U}_2^\top) = \mathbf{Q}.
$$

Using the orthonormality property of the eigenvectors, multiplying the equation on the left by $\mathbf{U}_1^\top$ and on the right by $\mathbf{U}_2$, we get

$$
\mathbf{V}_1(\mathbf{U}_1^\top \mathbf{B}_{12}\mathbf{U}_2) + (\mathbf{U}_1^\top \mathbf{B}_{12}\mathbf{U}_2)\mathbf{V}_2 = \mathbf{U}_1^\top \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{U}_2.
$$

Let $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{U}_1^\top \mathbf{B}_{12}\mathbf{U}_2$ so that the expression above can be written as $\mathbf{V}_1\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{V}_2 = \mathbf{U}_1^\top \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{U}_2$. Because $\mathbf{V}_1$ and $\mathbf{V}_2$ are diagonal, this equation can be solved elementwise as
$$
w_{ij} = \frac{(\mathbf{U}_1^\top \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{U}_2)_{ij}}{(\mathbf{V}_1)_{ii}+(\mathbf{V}_2)_{jj}}.
$$

Finally, multiplying again the left and right sides by $\mathbf{U}_1$ and $\mathbf{U}_2^\top$, respectively, the solution becomes
$$
\mathbf{B}_{12} = \mathbf{U}_1\mathbf{W}\mathbf{U}_2^\top.
$$

## Retraction

After computing the Riemannian gradient, the remaining problem is to map $\mathbf{X}_{k} - t\mathrm{grad}f(\mathbf{X}_k)$ back onto the orthoblique manifold. For this, we need to find a function $R_{\mathbf{X}_k}: \mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{X}_k}\mathcal{POB} \rightarrow \mathcal{POB}$ that satisfies the conditions of Definition \ref{retraction_definition} such that
$$
\mathbf{X}_{k+1}
=
R_{\mathbf{X}_k}
\left(
-t_k
\mathrm{grad}f(\mathbf{X}_k)
\right) \in \mathcal{POB}.
$$

For clarity, let $\mathbf{Z}$ denote the tangent step $\mathbf{X}_{k} - t\mathrm{grad}f(\mathbf{X}_k)$ and let $\mathbf{R}$ be the retracted update $\mathbf{X}_{k+1}$. Let us partition these matrices into blocks $\mathbf{Z} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{Z}_1 & \mathbf{Z}_2 & \mathbf{Z}_3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_1 & \mathbf{R}_2 & \mathbf{R}_3 \end{bmatrix}$ such that the matrices indexed by $1$ and $2$ correspond to the first two oblique blocks, respectively, and those indexed by $3$ correspond to the block of orthogonal factors.

The retraction of the first oblique block can be simply the retraction onto the oblique manifold with normalized columns $\mathbf{R}_1 = \mathbf{Z}_1 \left[ \mathrm{ddiag} \left( \mathbf{Z}_1^\top\mathbf{Z}_1 \right) \right]^{-1/2}$, with $\text{diag}(\mathbf{R}_1^\top \mathbf{R}_1) = \mathbf{1}$.

The second oblique block only has to be made orthogonal to the first block. We may use the Gram-Schmidt process to orthogonalize each column of $\mathbf{Z}_2$ with respect to all the columns of $\mathbf{Z}_1$ ^[This is like doing a QR decomposition of $\mathbf{Z}_1$ with each column of $\mathbf{Z}_2$ appended to $\mathbf{Z}_1$ in turn.]. This process may be computationally expensive when there are many blocks of factors, so a better retraction is to project $\mathbf{Z}_2$ onto the orthogonal space of $\mathbf{Z}_1$. First, define the orthogonal projector onto the column space of $\mathbf{R}_1$ as $\mathbf{P}_1 = \mathbf{R}_1 \left( \mathbf{R}_1^\top\mathbf{R}_1 \right)^{-1} \mathbf{R}_1^\top$. Then, $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_2 = \left( \mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_1 \right) \mathbf{Z}_2$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{R}_1$. Second, the columns are subsequently normalized to obtain 
$$
\mathbf{R}_2 = \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_2 \left[ \mathrm{ddiag} \left( \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_2^\top \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_2 \right) \right]^{-1/2}.
$$ 
Consequently, $\mathbf{R}_1^\top\mathbf{R}_2 = \mathbf{0}$ and $\text{diag} \left( \mathbf{R}_2^\top\mathbf{R}_2 \right) = \mathbf{1}$.

Finally, to get $\mathbf{R}_3$, combine the two oblique blocks columnwise in $\mathbf{R}_{12} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_1 & \mathbf{R}_2 \end{bmatrix}$ and define the projector onto their joint column space, $\mathbf{P}_{12} = \mathbf{R}_{12} \left( \mathbf{R}_{12}^\top \mathbf{R}_{12} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{R}_{12}^\top$. As before, the orthogonal block is first projected onto the orthogonal complement of both oblique blocks to yield $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_3 = \left( \mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{12} \right) \mathbf{Z}_3$ and its columns are then orthonormalized using 
$$
\mathbf{R}_3 = \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_3 \left( \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_3^\top \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_3 \right)^{-1/2}
$$
As a result, $\mathbf{R}_1^\top\mathbf{R}_3 = \mathbf{0}, \qquad \mathbf{R}_2^\top\mathbf{R}_3 = \mathbf{0}, \qquad \mathbf{R}_3^\top\mathbf{R}_3 = \mathbf{I}$.

With $\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{V}$, the same blockwise construction defines the retracted update
$$
R_{\mathbf{X}}^{\mathcal{POB}}(\mathbf{V}) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_1 & \mathbf{R}_2 & \mathbf{R}_3 \end{bmatrix}.
$$
For nonsingular $\mathbf{X}$ and sufficiently small tangent steps, the required Gram matrices remain positive definite, so the construction is smooth. At $\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{0}$, the normalizations leave all blocks unchanged and the projections remove nothing, so $R_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{X}$. To check the second condition, take $\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{X}+t\mathbf{V}$ with $\mathbf{V}$ tangent. Its blockwise crossproducts satisfy
$$
\mathbf{Z}_i^\top\mathbf{Z}_j
=\mathbf{X}_i^\top\mathbf{X}_j
+t\left(\mathbf{X}_i^\top\mathbf{V}_j+\mathbf{V}_i^\top\mathbf{X}_j\right)
+t^2\mathbf{V}_i^\top\mathbf{V}_j.
$$
Tangency eliminates the coefficient of $t$ in every constrained entry. Thus, normalizing the first block only adds corrections of quadratic or higher order. The crossproduct $\mathbf{R}_1^\top\mathbf{Z}_2$ still begins at quadratic order, and hence so does $\mathbf{P}_1\mathbf{Z}_2$, since the other factors in the projector formula are smooth and bounded. The same argument applies to normalizing the second block and to projecting and orthonormalizing the third. All corrections therefore leave the first-order term $t\mathbf{V}$ unchanged, giving $\mathrm{D}R_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{0})[\mathbf{V}]=\mathbf{V}$.

Any fixed block order also satisfies these retraction conditions, provided each block is projected onto the orthogonal complement of all previously processed blocks and then normalized or orthonormalized as appropriate. Different orders may produce different finite updates but preserve the same initial direction. This does not permit arbitrary exchanges of individual operations: projecting an already normalized block generally requires normalization again.

## Generalization to an arbitrary number of oblique blocks

The previous construction of the orthoblique manifold can be extended to any number $m$ of oblique blocks. Let $p_i$ be the number of factors in the $i$th oblique block and let $r$ be the number of completely orthogonal factors, so that $n=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i+r$. Then,

$$
\mathcal{POB}\big(\{p_1,\ldots,p_m\},r\big) = \left\{\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}: \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{Y}_1 & \mathbf{0} & \dots  & \mathbf{0} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \mathbf{0} & \vdots \\
\vdots & \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{Y}_m & \mathbf{0} \\
\mathbf{0} & \dots & \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I} \\
\end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{diag}(\mathbf{Y}_i) = \mathbf{1} \ \forall i
\right\}.
$$

In this setup, the tangent space, normal space, and retraction would involve additional oblique blocks, pairs of oblique blocks, and pairs of oblique and orthogonal blocks. But all the formulas of these quantities follow by applying the same blockwise approach as before.

Furthermore, this generalization shows that orthogonal and oblique rotations are special cases of the orthoblique manifold. If there are no oblique blocks and $r=n$, then $\mathcal{POB}(\varnothing,n)=\mathcal{O}(n)$. And if there is one oblique block with $p_1=n$ and $r=0$, then $\mathcal{POB}(\{n\},0)=\mathcal{OB}(n)$.

Table \ref{tab:gpa-comparison} brings together the common GPA steps and the geometric differences between orthogonal, oblique, and orthoblique rotation. It also distinguishes the quantities used to derive the projected gradient from the operations used to update $\mathbf{X}$.

# Rotation constraints and standard errors

We already know how to impose constraints on $\mathbf{X}$ in each orthogonal, oblique, and orthoblique rotation scenarios. A remaining matter is how these constraints are translated to the rotated loadings $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ and factor correlation matrix $\mathbf{\Psi}$.

At any tangent direction $\mathbf{V}$, we should have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{D}f(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}] &= \langle \Delta f_\mathbf{\Lambda\Psi}, \text{D}\zeta(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}]\rangle, \\
&= 0, \quad \text{at convergence.}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-differential_rotated}
where $\Delta f_\mathbf{\Lambda\Psi}$ is the gradient of the complexity function with respect to the rotated parameters and $\zeta$ is the function that transform the rotation matrix into the rotated parameters. More importantly, the second equality follows because at a given solution the complexity criterion must be stationary.

In orthogonal rotation, the rotated loadings are $\mathbf{\Lambda} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_0\mathbf{X}$. As we already showed, a tangent direction in this manifold can be written as $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\Omega}$ for an skew-symmetric $\mathbf{\Omega}$. Then, the directional derivative of the rotated loadings is $\mathrm{D}\zeta(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}] = \mathbf{\Lambda}_0\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{\Omega}$. Substituting these expressions in @eq-differential_rotated and equaling to zero we have
$$
\langle \Delta f_\mathbf{\Lambda}, \mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{\Omega}\rangle = \langle \mathbf{\Omega}, \mathbf{\Lambda}^\top\Delta f_{\Lambda}\rangle = 0.
$$
Now, because $\mathbf{\Omega}$ is skew-symmetric, it follows that $\mathbf{\Lambda}^\top\Delta f_{\Lambda}$ must be symmetric.

In oblique rotation, the rotated parameters become $\zeta(\mathbf{X}) = \{\mathbf{\Lambda} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_0\mathbf{X}^{-\top}, \mathbf{\Psi} = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\}$. A tangent direction in this manifold can be written as $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}$ for an off-diagonal $\mathbf{\Omega}$. Then, by substitutions the directional derivative of the rotated parameters are
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{D}\zeta(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}]
&= \{-\mathbf{\Lambda}_0\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{X}^{-\top}, \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{V} + \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{X}\} \\
&= \{-\mathbf{\Lambda} (\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega})^{\top} \mathbf{X}^{-\top}, \mathbf{X}^\top (\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}) + (\mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega})^\top \mathbf{X}\} \\
&= \{-\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{\Omega}^\top\mathbf{\Psi}^{-1}, \mathbf{\Omega} + \mathbf{\Omega}^\top \} .
\end{aligned}
$$
Finally, substituting these expressions in @eq-differential_rotated and equaling to zero we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \langle \Delta f_\mathbf{\Lambda}, -\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{\Omega}^\top\mathbf{\Psi}^{-1} \rangle + \langle \Delta f_\mathbf{\Psi}, \mathbf{\Omega} + \mathbf{\Omega}^\top \rangle, \\
&= \mathrm{trace}(-\Delta f_\mathbf{\Lambda}^\top \mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{\Omega}^\top\mathbf{\Psi}^{-1}) + \mathrm{trace}(\Delta f_\mathbf{\Psi}^\top (\mathbf{\Omega} + \mathbf{\Omega}^\top)), \\
&= \mathrm{trace}(-\mathbf{\Psi}^{-1}\Delta f_\mathbf{\Lambda}^\top \mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{\Omega}^\top) + \mathrm{trace}(2\Delta f_\mathbf{\Psi} \mathbf{\Omega}^\top).
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\Delta f_\mathbf{\Psi}$ is symmetric. Now, because $\mathbf{\Omega}$ is off-diagonal and its orthogonal complement is any diagonal matrix, it follows that $2\Delta f_\mathbf{\Psi} -\mathbf{\Psi}^{-1}\Delta f_\mathbf{\Lambda}^\top \mathbf{\Lambda}$ must be diagonal.

The rotation constraints of the diagonal blocks of the orthoblique manifold are the same than those of the oblique and orthogonal manifolds. We only need to derive the constraints for the intersections between the oblique-oblique blocks and oblique-orthogonal blocks.

Notice that the rotated parameters in the orthoblique rotation follow the same parameterization than in oblique rotation, $\zeta(\mathbf{X}) = \{\mathbf{\Lambda} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_0\mathbf{X}^{-\top}, \mathbf{\Psi} = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\}$. The tangent space of the orthoblique manifold also has the form $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X}^{-\top}\mathbf{\Omega}$, but $\mathbf{\Omega}$ is not generally skew-symmetric like inorthogonal rotation nor off-diagonal like in oblique rotation. Instead, the blocks of oblique factors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$ are arbitrary off-diagonal matrices, the block of orthogonal factors in $\mathbf{\Omega}$ is skew-symmetric, and the intersections in $\mathbf{\Omega}$ between different blocks of factors $i$ and $j$ satisfy $\mathbf{\Omega}_{ij}=-\mathbf{\Omega}_{ji}^\top$ (i.e., they are arbitrary but skew-symmetric in the full $\mathbf{\Omega}$). Therefore,
$$
\mathrm{D}\zeta(\mathbf{X})[\mathbf{V}] = \{-\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{\Omega}^\top\mathbf{\Psi}^{-1}, \mathbf{\Omega} + \mathbf{\Omega}^\top \},
$$
and $2\Delta f_\mathbf{\Psi} -\mathbf{\Psi}^{-1}\Delta f_\mathbf{\Lambda}^\top \mathbf{\Lambda}$ must be symmetric, with the submatrices corresponding to the blocks of oblique factors being also diagonal.

# Software: orthoblique rotation with the latent package

A general rotation framework should allow researchers to compare and use different factor structures without developing a new optimization routine for each application. The \texttt{GPArotation} package already provides this framework for conventional orthogonal and oblique rotation, with a wide catalogue of rotation criteria. These are features retained in our \texttt{latent} package, with some additional capabilities. The relevant innovation here is the addition of the orthoblique manifold to restrict the factor-correlation structure as desired and the application of different rotation criteria to different blocks of factors.

Rotation in the \texttt{latent} package is performed through the \texttt{lrotate()} function, which can receive an initial loading matrix and factor correlation matrix to be rotated. An example is presented below:
```{r}
#| label: software-lrotate
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
library(latent)
# Orthogonal factor rotation with varimax:
fit_rotation <- lrotate(lambda = unrotated_lambda,
                        projection = "orth",
                        rotation = "varimax")
```

As it can be seen, the choice of criterion is separated from the choice of geometry: \texttt{rotation} specifies the criterion, whereas \texttt{projection} selects between orthogonal (\texttt{"orth"}), oblique (\texttt{"oblq"}), and orthoblique (\texttt{"poblq"}) manifolds. 

<!-- The implemented criteria include the Crawford--Ferguson family, oblimin, geomin, and target rotations.  -->

For the block structure developed in this paper, consider the following orthoblique target rotation:
```{r}
#| label: software-lrotate-poblq
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
library(latent)
# Orthoblique target rotation:
fit_rotation <- lrotate(lambda = unrotated_lambda,
                        projection = "poblq", oblique = c(3, 3),
                        rotation = "target", target = target)
```

Here, The \texttt{"poblq"} permits correlations within prespecified blocks of factors while retaining exact orthogonality between blocks, whereas \texttt{oblique} specifies the sizes of consecutive oblique blocks. For instance, with six factors, \texttt{oblique = c(3, 3)} gives two different oblique blocks of three factors with zero between-block correlations. If $\texttt{unrotated\_lambda}$ contained more than 6 columns, then any remaining factor would automatically be treated as orthogonal.

As an alternative to \texttt{lrotate()}, the function \texttt{lefa()} for exploratory factor analysis takes the raw data or a covariance matrix as inputs and performs factor extraction first and rotation later. \texttt{lefa()} allows all the same arguments as \texttt{lrotate()} but contains additional choices for factor extraction with either maximum likelihood (\texttt{"ml"}), unweighted least-squares (\texttt{"uls"}), or diagonally-weighted least-squares (\texttt{"dwls"}) for ordinal data.
```{r}
#| label: software-lefa
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
# Oblique EFA with Maximum Likelihood and oblique oblimin rotation:
fit_efa <- lefa(data = data.matrix,
                sample.cov = NULL, # Optional covariance matrix
                nfactors = 6L, 
                estimator = "ml",
                projection = "oblq",
                rotation = "oblimin")
```

Because different factor blocks may contain different levels of complexity, both \texttt{lrotate} and \texttt{lefa()} allow the application of different rotation criteria to arbitrary columns of $\mathbf{\Lambda}$. Suppose that we have a block of three oblique factors and another block of three orthogonal factors. Then, we may choose to apply oblimin to the oblique block to maximize item simplicity but varimax to the orthogonal block to maximize the variance of the squared loadings within factors. This rotation specification can be easily implemented by providing a list of rotation criteria to the \texttt{rotation} argument:
```{r}
#| label: software-lrotate-blocks
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
# Orthoblique EFA with combined oblimin + varimax rotations:
fit_efa <- lefa(data = data.matrix,
                nfactors = 6L, 
                estimator = "ml",
                projection = "poblq", oblique = 3,
                rotation = list(
                  oblimin = list(factors = 1:3),
                  varimax = list(factors = 4:6)))
```

Notice that we only had to specify a single number in the \texttt{oblique} argument to let GPA know that only the first three factors are indeed oblique and every other factor is orthogonal. Then, in the \texttt{rotation} argument the oblimin criterion is applied to the first three columns of $\mathbf{\Lambda}$, which corresponds to the oblique factors, whereas the varimax is applied to the last three columns, corresponding to the orthogonal factors.

The development version of \texttt{latent}, including the source and documentation of \texttt{lrotate()} and \texttt{lefa()} functions, is available at \url{https://github.com/Marcosjnez/latent}. You can install the package with the command \texttt{pak::pak("marcosjnez/latent")}.

# Empirical applications

We now illustrate the use of the orthoblique manifold with two empirical applications in which neither a fully orthogonal nor a fully oblique rotation would represent the intended factor-correlation structure. The examples come from psychopathology and personality research. In both cases, we used target rotation, so the theoretical factor structure provides a starting point for the analyses, but we do not take these theoretical structures for granted. Instead, EFA will deliver a result that may agree or not with the target. In this regards, EFA becomes useful because the substantive structure provides information about the expected orientation of the factors, but there is no reason to assume that all secondary loadings are exactly zero or that all the items are true indicators of their theoretical factors.

In the psychopathology example, we use a multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) design, where the same traits are measured using different informants. In these models, the associations between indicators may arise from the substantive traits but also from the method through which the measurements were obtained. Here, child, parent, and teacher reports constitute the different methods. EFA allows us to examine whether the expected trait structure emerges without fixing the loading pattern, whereas the orthoblique manifold keeps trait and method sources of common variance separated by imposing orthogonality between both blocks of factors.

In the personality example, the HEXACO hierarchy contains many items and factors. It is therefore plausible that some items have secondary loadings or that some facets are less clearly defined than expected. EFA allows these possibilities to be examined instead of assuming that every item belongs exclusively to its designated domain and facet. However, the distinction between general and specific factors still requires selected factor correlations to be zero. Thus, the exploratory model leaves all loadings free, whereas the orthoblique manifold constrains to zero the correlations between general and specific factors, as well as the correlations between specific factors belonging to different blocks.

Thus, both examples can be studied exploratorily while preserving the theoretically specified zero correlations between theoretically unrelated factors.

All analyses were conducted with the `latent` package and the `lefa()` function.

## ASEBA. An exploratory Multitrait-multimethod model

The first application uses the MTMM data analyzed by @watts_2022. The correlation matrix was obtained from the supplementary materials available at <https://osf.io/hvskz/>. We used the ABCD sample ($N=2,119$), which includes child-, parent-, and teacher-reported psychopathology indicators measuring three traits: Attention Problems, Externalizing, and Internalizing. ^[The original data included 56 indicators but two duplicated indicators (\texttt{ARGUc} and \texttt{ARGUp}) were identified after noticing the correlation matrix was not positive-definite. These indicators were removed from the supplied correlation matrix as we did not know to which method factor they would correspond, leaving 54 indicators available for the current analysis.]

The original authors included the Attention Problems indicators in an Externalizing factor [@watts_2022]. This decision had a substantive motivation. Although the Achenbach System of Empirically Based Assessment (ASEBA) does not include Attention Problems in its Externalizing composite, @watts_2022 included these indicators because attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is widely regarded as a marker of childhood Externalizing. They also referred to previous ASEBA analyses in which Attention Problems loaded strongly on an Externalizing factor. An exploratory analysis can examine whether the Attention Problems indicators are adequately captured by the Externalizing factor, as assumed in the merged specification.

Following the specification used by @watts_2022, the attention-problems indicators were included with Externalizing. We therefore considered five exploratory factors: two trait factors corresponding to Externalizing and Internalizing, where the Externalizing label now includes the items of the Attention Problems factor, and three method factors corresponding to children, parents, and teachers. 

Each indicator is expected to reflect both a substantive trait and a measurement method, but this allocation need not hold exactly in the data. Some indicators may show secondary loadings or may represent their designated trait or method less clearly than expected. An exploratory partially specified target rotation allows these possibilities to be examined without fixing non-target loadings to zero. At the same time, the MTMM structure requires trait factors to remain uncorrelated with method factors, while correlations may be allowed among trait factors and among method factors. Thus, the target criterion provides the substantive orientation of the factors, whereas the orthoblique manifold constrains all trait–method factor correlations to zero.

The two trait factors and the three method factors form two internally oblique blocks such that
$$
\boldsymbol{\Psi}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{T} & \mathbf{0}\\
\mathbf{0} & \boldsymbol{\Psi}_{M}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus, the Externalizing-Internalizing correlation and the three correlations among method factors are estimated, whereas all six trait-method correlations are constrained to zero by the orthoblique manifold.

The model was fitted using unweighted least squares and target rotation as follows:
```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
set.seed(2026)
R <- mtmm$ABCD$R # Extract the correlation matrix
efa <- lefa(sample.cov = R, sample.nobs = 2119,
            nfactors = 5, estimator = "uls",
            projection = "poblq", oblique = c(2, 3),
            rotation = "target", target = Target)
```

The results showed that the estimated correlation between Externalizing and Internalizing was .251. The correlations were .298 between Children and Parents, .240 between Children and Teachers, and .302 between Parents and Teachers. In contrast, all six correlations between trait and method factors were zero to numerical precision as expected by the orthoblique constraints. 

The partially specified target rotation produced a sparse loading pattern. Among the 162 loadings targeted toward zero, 160 (98.8\%) had absolute values below .20, with a median absolute value of .030. The method factors were particularly well defined: all 54 expected method loadings exceeded .20 in absolute value, with a median absolute loading of .464. In contrast, the Externalizing indicators, apart from those assessing Attention Problems, loaded poorly on the merged trait factor. Of these 18 indicators, 16 had absolute loadings below .20, with a median of .079 and a range from .028 to .259. In contrast, 15 of the 18 Attention Problems indicators exceeded .20 on the same factor, with a median absolute loading of .433. Thereby, the original Externalizing indicators contributed little to the merged trait factor, which was mainly defined by Attention Problems. 

Moreover, all 18 original Externalizing indicators loaded more strongly on their corresponding method factor than on the merged trait factor, with a median absolute method loading of .530. Therefore, their weak trait loadings do not mean that they contributed little to the entire solution. Rather, their shared variation was represented more strongly by the method factors, while the merged trait factor mainly reflected Attention Problems and not Externalizing. 

Overall, this exploratory solution revealed that conflating the indicators of Externalizing and Attention problems in a single factor did not recover the intended broad representation of both sets of indicators. As such, retaining the Externalizing label for this merged factor was not appropriate as only the original indicators of Attention Problems loaded on the factor.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\captionsetup{width=1\textwidth}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{"examples/multitrait_multimethod/target (loadings).pdf"}
\caption{\fontsize{12}{12}\selectfont Absolute values of factor loadings for the multitrait-multimethod analysis.}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\captionsetup{width=1\textwidth}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{"examples/multitrait_multimethod/target (correlations).pdf"}
\caption{\fontsize{12}{12}\selectfont Absolute values of factor correlations for the multitrait-multimethod analysis.}
\end{figure}

From a statistical perspective, the relevant feature of this example is that rotation criteria and restrictions on the factor correlation matrix are handled separately. Target rotation determines an interpretable orientation and permits empirically relevant cross-loadings, whereas the orthoblique manifold guarantees the exact block-orthogonality structure that disentangles the variance explained by traits and methods. A conventional orthogonal rotation would have forced the correlations within the trait and method blocks to zero, while a conventional oblique rotation would have estimated the six trait-method correlations that must be excluded by the MTMM design. In both cases, the results would have been inconsistent with the theoretical model. Thus, the orthoblique manifold combined with target rotation made possible to test with EFA the adequacy of this MTMM analysis, revealing a possible modeling misspecification in @watts_2022.

Finally, we also consider it important to mention that this use of target rotation is closely related to the extended target rotation proposed by @zhang_2019 for MTMM data. Their method incorporates expectations about both the loading matrix and the factor correlation matrix into the rotation criterion (i.e., extended target rotation), so that selected trait-method correlations are rotated toward zero. Actually, the extended target rotation should be almost equivalent to target rotation with the orthoblique manifold. However, the manifold and rotation roles are separated in our new approach: the target criterion is used only to orient the loading matrix, while the orthoblique manifold imposes the trait-method orthogonality exactly. Hence, the correlations encouraged to be small by extended target rotation in @zhang_2019 are represented here as exact structural restrictions of the rotation manifold. As such, a benefit of our approach with regard to the extended target rotation is that the constant parameter that weights the relative contribution of target loadings and target correlations is not required.

## HEXACO. A hierarchical mode with multiple oblique general factors

The second application uses the `icases` data obtained from the repository accompanying @anglim_2022 at <https://osf.io/72zp3/>. We selected the MOOC sample ($N=4,286$), an international sample of participants who completed the HEXACO-100. The original study reports that the sample included participants from 131 countries, with 69\% being female, and had a mean age of 34.7 years. For the present analysis, we used 96 HEXACO items corresponding to the six personality domains and their 24 facets, excluding the last four altruism items that do not belong to the HEXACO hierarchy (i.e, they are not expected to be nested in a general factor).

We fitted a 30-factor EFA model with six general factors, one for each HEXACO domain, and 24 specific factors. The first six factors were specified as one oblique block and the 24 specific factors were left orthogonal. The resulting factor correlation matrix has the form
$$
\boldsymbol{\Psi}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{G} & \mathbf{0}\\
\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I}_{24}
\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{G}$ contains the correlations among the six domain-general factors. Therefore, the general factors can correlate, whereas every specific factor is orthogonal to the general factors and to all other specific factors. This manner, common variance would be partitioned between specific factors, representing narrow facet-level variance, and general factors, representing broader variance shared across facets.

This formulation extends the exploratory bifactor approach of Jennrich and Bentler (2011; 2012) to the case of multiple correlated general factors. In their biquartimin and bigeomin criteria, a single general-factor column is excluded from the simplicity rotation criterion, which is applied to the group-factor columns only. Here, there are six general-factor columns, and their orientation also has to be determined. We therefore applied a criterion to the general factor columns and another to the specific factor columns. Thus this example also illustrates the possibility of combining different rotation criteria within the same analysis. 

To examine the extent to which the theoretical HEXACO structure is sound, there were many possible choices for analysis. Because there are 30 factors in total, a nontarget rotation has a large rotational search space and hence there exists the risk that we capitalize on chance. On the other hand, because the target matrix would constrain a large number of loadings toward zero, the analysis would become more confirmatory than intended. Therefore, four alternative specifications were fitted to explore how the recovered HEXACO structure varied across rotation criteria: geomin for the general and specific factors, oblimin for the general and specific factors, geomin for the general factors combined with target rotation for the specific factors, and oblimin for the general factors combined with target rotation for the specific factors.^[We set the oblimin parameter $\gamma$ to $0$ in all the analyses, so the criterion becomes quartimin. For geomin, we set $\epsilon=.01$ in all the analyses. For the analyses with the target rotation, the target used the known HEXACO facet memberships to anchor the orientation of the specific factors.] Because the specific-factor block was considerably larger and more complex than the general-factor block, target rotation was applied only to the specific factors in the target-based specifications, providing theoretical anchoring where rotational complexity was greatest. In the specifications without target rotation, the specific factors were rotated using the same rotation criterion as the general factors (i.e., oblimin or geomin). As such, these latter configurations can be seen as generalizations of the biquartimin and bigeomin criteria developed by Jennrich and Bentler (2011; 2012). 

In the end, it was reassuring to see that the results of all the analyses converged overall. On the one hand, in both target-based specifications all 96 items had their largest absolute loading among the 24 specific factors on the theoretically-expected facet. When target rotation was not applied, this occurred for 72 of 96 items with geomin on the specific factors and for 73 of 96 items with oblimin on the specific factors. On the other hand, the correspondence with the expected facet structure was substantial even under the nontarget specifications: 75.0\% of the items with geomin and 76.0\% with oblimin had their largest absolute specific-factor loading on the corresponding facet. The broad recovery of the facet pattern was therefore not solely a consequence of applying a target. Nevertheless, this correspondence was not complete. Whereas the target specifications largely confirmed the expected HEXACO structure, the nontarget rotations may additionally provide insights into which facets and items may need further attention. Facets whose designated items have small loadings should be subjected to a closer examination of their content or item placement.

The general-factor loading patterns also broadly reflected the HEXACO domains across the four analyses. The item sets for Emotionality, Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Openness, and Agreeableness were recognizable in each solution, whereas Honesty--Humility was less consistently separated, especially in the target-based specifications. Some Honesty--Humility items showed salient cross-loadings on the Conscientiousness general factor, and additional general-factor cross-loadings remained. Thus, agreement across rotations was substantial but did not imply equally clear recovery of every domain. Because none of the four specifications targeted the general-factor loadings, this broad correspondence was not imposed directly by the target, although targeting the specific factors could still alter the partitioning of common variance.

For brevity, we interpret further only the oblimin + target solution.^[To check the other solutions, see the repository https://github.com/Marcosjnez/orthoblique.] Here, oblimin was applied to the six general factors, leaving their loading pattern exploratory, whereas target rotation was applied to the 24 specific factors. Because the items are ordinal, the model was estimated with diagonally weighted least squares using polychoric correlations. The selected specification was fitted as follows:
```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
rotation_model <- list(
  oblimin = list(gamma = 0, factors = 1:6),
  target = list(target = Target[, 7:30], factors = 7:30)
)
efa <- lefa(data = mooc, nfactors = 30,
            ordered = TRUE, estimator = "dwls",
            projection = "poblq", oblique = 6,
            rotation = rotation_model)
```

The results showed that the absolute correlations among the six general factors ranged from .006 to .218, with a median of .107. All general-specific correlations and all off-diagonal correlations among the 24 specific factors were zero to numerical precision, as expected by the orthoblique constraints. Therefore, of the $30(29)/2=435$ possible factor correlations, only the $6(5)/2=15$ correlations among the general factors were estimated, while the remaining 420 were exactly zero.

The six general factors remained substantially exploratory in this analysis. The median absolute loading on the theoretically-expected general factor was .385; 85 of the 96 designated general-factor loadings exceeded .20 in absolute value, and 430 of the 480 general-factor cross-loadings (89.6\%) were below .20. For the 24 specific factors, the median absolute theoretically expected loading was .430, and 91 of these 96 loadings exceeded .20. In contrast, 2,205 of the 2,208 specific-factor cross-loadings (99.86\%) were below .20, and no cross-loading exceeded .30.

\centering
\captionsetup{width=1\textwidth}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{"examples/correlated_general_factors/oblimin + target (loadings).pdf"}
\caption{\fontsize{12}{12}\selectfont Absolute values of factor loadings for the HEXACO oblimin + target solution.}
\end{figure}

\captionsetup{width=1\textwidth}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{"examples/correlated_general_factors/oblimin + target (correlations).pdf"}
\caption{\fontsize{12}{12}\selectfont Absolute values of factor correlations for the HEXACO oblimin + target solution.}

The conceptual advantage of the orthoblique manifold was particularly clear in this example. A fully oblique 30-factor rotation would allow all 435 factor correlations, although only the 15 correlations among the six general factors are needed for this representation. Conversely, a fully orthogonal rotation would force these 15 correlations to zero. At the same time, the mixed rotation criterion leaves the six general factors under a less restrictive simplicity criterion and uses the target only where the large number of specific factors makes theoretical anchoring desirable, reducing the risk of capitalizing on chance.

Taken together, these applications illustrate the distinction between rotation criteria and manifold restrictions. Complexity criteria can yield different sparsity and parsimony patterns for each block of factors whereas the orthoblique manifold defines the admissible factor-correlation geometry exactly. The two mechanisms can therefore be combined without turning the factor model into a confirmatory simple-structure model.

# Conclusion

Until now, conventional GPA-based factor rotation has generally treated factors as either completely orthogonal or completely oblique. We developed the orthoblique rotation to allow oblique blocks of factors to coexist with exact orthogonality between selected blocks. The empirical applications illustrated two complementary uses of this geometry: an MTMM representation in which trait and method factors can correlate within their respective blocks while remaining orthogonal between blocks, and a general-specific personality representation in which several general factors may correlate while remaining orthogonal to the specific factors, which are also mutually orthogonal.

We also provided a detailed and self-contained review of the GPA, connecting its computational steps with the geometry of the rotation constraints. In particular, starting from the defining constraints, we derived the tangent and normal spaces and used their orthogonal decomposition to establish the Riemannian gradient for orthoblique rotation. The conventional orthogonal and oblique formulas can be recovered within the same account, so orthoblique rotation can be regarded as a generalization of orthogonal and oblique rotations. Therefore, the orthogonal and oblique manifolds are not competing constructions that must be replaced, but special cases of the more general orthoblique manifold. We hope that these explicit connections make factor rotation a less obscure matter in factor analysis and help researchers understand how further extensions can be constructed.

In the end, this extension should be understood as a continuation of the general rotation program developed by @jennrich_2001, @jennrich_2002, and Bernaards and Jennrich 2005. Moreover, the empirical analyses on data with multiple general factors illustrated that the current work can also be viewed as a continuation of the bifactor exploratory analysis methods with biquartimin and bigeomin [@jennrich_2011; @jennrich_2012]. A central insight of Jennrich was that the same algorithm could optimize many simplicity criteria. Here, we showed how the same geometric reasoning can also accommodate different patterns of factor-correlation constraints. 

Additionally, we provided a new R package to exploit these new rotation capabilities. \texttt{lefa()} combines factor extraction and \texttt{lrotate()} in a single call. This makes the same orthoblique specification available when the analysis starts from raw data or a sample covariance matrix. Through the \texttt{projection}, \texttt{oblique}, and \texttt{rotation} arguments, researchers can specify the factor-correlation blocks and the criteria applied to their loadings within the same analysis. Consequently, the proposed extension is already available for use.

We hope that the combination of the orthoblique manifold with mixed rotation criteria considerably expands the range of possible rotation specifications. Different assumptions about factor correlations can be combined with different simplicity criteria for the corresponding loading blocks. The present applications illustrate only a few of these combinations; we have not examined the many other possibilities or established which will be most useful in different substantive settings. The \texttt{latent} package makes these unexplored combinations already available to researchers, who can investigate new rotation configurations based on their parameter recovery, stability, and interpretability. In this sense, the current work provides both a geometric construction and a software basis for further research on factor rotation and, more broadly, on ESEM.
